title: Diwali Sweets Will Cost More as Ghee, Sugar and Dry Fruit Prices Climb
excerpt: Sweet shops across India are preparing to pass on surging ingredient costs this festive season — and shoppers may pay more or get smaller boxes.
body:
• Retail sugar prices averaged ₹62 per kg in September, up from ₹47 in June, while milk, desi ghee and dry fruit costs have all climbed ahead of Diwali.
  • Sweet makers report dairy input costs up 8–15%, and brands like Bikaji Foods say sugar procurement is running about 20% above budgeted levels.
  • Companies are weighing price hikes of 2–5% or shrinkflation — smaller packs at the same price — to protect margins during the festive peak.
  • A shortfall in sugar production has pushed the government to permit raw sugar imports for the first time in about a decade and impose stock limits.

Diwali mithai is about to get more expensive. Sweet shops across India are preparing to pass on a surge in ingredient costs — from desi ghee and dry fruits to sugar and milk — that has squeezed margins through the year's biggest selling season, according to The Tribune and industry reports.

The price pressure is broad-based. The all-India average retail price of sugar stood at ₹62 per kg in September, up from ₹47 in June, Ministry of Consumer Affairs data shows. In Maharashtra, retail prices have crossed ₹65 per kg. Milk prices in Mumbai rose ₹9 per litre from September 1, and sweet makers report that raw milk, khoya and ghee costs are up 8–15% over seasonal baselines.

Why prices are climbing

Sugar is the single biggest driver. Government estimates put sugar production for the current October–September season at around 306 lakh metric tonnes, well below the initial estimate of about 343 lakh metric tonnes, as pest infestation and waterlogging hit cane. Nearly 30 lakh tonnes have been diverted for ethanol, tightening supplies further, and India's sugar recovery rate has slipped from around 10% in 2022 to 9.3% this year, according to Crisil Intelligence.

The government has responded with unusual measures: it has permitted raw sugar imports for the first time in about a decade and introduced stock limits to contain prices. Pushan Sharma, director at Crisil Intelligence, said the measures could bridge the immediate demand-supply gap during the festive season but may not offer lasting relief.

Dairy inputs are the second squeeze. Traditional sweets rely heavily on concentrated milk solids, and khoya and mawa — the evaporated milk solids at the heart of barfi, peda and gulab jamun — have seen sharp escalation on tighter seasonal milk supplies and stronger institutional demand. Packaging materials, commercial gas and transport costs are compounding the hit for small confectioners and large chains alike.

What it means for shoppers

For festive shoppers, the choice will be familiar: pay more, or get less for the same money. Bikaji Foods is rolling out an approximately 2% price increase across its sweets portfolio, its CFO Rishabh Jain told the Times of India, noting that sugar procurement costs remain around 20% higher than they were a few months ago.

"Sugar procurement costs remain around 20% higher than they were a few months ago."

— Rishabh Jain, CFO, Bikaji Foods, to the Times of India

Industry executives say companies could respond with 2–5% price hikes or shrinkflation — reducing pack sizes while holding prices steady. Trade bodies expect many regional sweet shops to pass through 5–10% increases on mithai categories, though manufacturers are wary of testing price-sensitive festive demand too hard. Some, like Parle Products, say they are focusing on operational efficiencies first rather than raising prices immediately.

The diaspora table

The squeeze travels with the festival. NRIs stocking up on mithai for Diwali parties — whether in Edison, London or Dubai — buy from the same supply chains, and higher input costs in India ripple into gift boxes and imported sweets abroad. With Diwali demand also lifting Indian food exports, overseas buyers are competing for the same kaju katli and laddoos at higher prices.

What to watch

The next test comes as Diwali demand peaks: whether the government's import and stock-limit measures keep retail sugar prices from climbing further, and whether sweet makers hold the line on prices or push through broader hikes. If sugar procurement stays elevated into the wedding season, the festive premium on mithai could linger well past Diwali.
